key_terms.meaning: An unordered collection of distinct objects, written with braces such as {1,2,3}.
A⊆B when every element of A is also an element of B; A=B needs A⊆B and B⊆A.
A∪B={x: x∈A or x∈B or both}.
Aᶜ=U∖A, where U is the fixed universal set.
A×B={(a,b): a∈A and b∈B}, a set of ordered pairs.
A subset of A×B; a relation on A is a subset of A×A.
R on A is reflexive when (a,a)∈R for every a∈A.
R on A is symmetric when (a,b)∈R implies (b,a)∈R.
R on A is antisymmetric when (a,b)∈R and (b,a)∈R imply a=b.
R on A is transitive when (a,b)∈R and (b,c)∈R imply (a,c)∈R.
The smallest transitive relation containing R; on a finite n-element set it is R∪R²∪…∪Rⁿ.
A triple-loop method that computes the transitive closure or reachability matrix in O(n³) time.
A relation on A that is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
For an equivalence relation ~, [a]={x∈A: x~a}.
A collection of nonempty pairwise disjoint subsets of A whose union is A.
A reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive relation on A, usually written a≤b.
A drawing of a finite poset with edges only for covering pairs, larger element above smaller.
A rule f:A→B that assigns exactly one element f(a)∈B to each a∈A.
A function that is both injective and surjective, so an inverse exists.
For bijective f:A→B, f⁻¹:B→A sends f(a) back to a.

takeaways: A set identity is proved by showing each side is a subset of the other; a membership table is only shorthand for the same element-wise check.
A relation on A is just a subset of A×A, so its ordered pairs, 0-1 matrix and digraph carry the same information.
Reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric and transitive are separate tests; asymmetric is stronger than antisymmetric, and asymmetric forces irreflexive.
The transitive closure is the smallest transitive relation containing R, and on a finite set it collects all paths of length 1 through n.
Warshall's algorithm fills an n×n reachability matrix in n³ steps by allowing intermediate vertices one by one.
An equivalence relation slices A into disjoint equivalence classes, and every partition of A comes from exactly one equivalence relation.
A partial order allows incomparable elements; a Hasse diagram keeps only covering pairs and drops all implied arrows.
A function is invertible exactly when it is bijective, and inversion reverses composition: (g∘f)⁻¹=f⁻¹∘g⁻¹.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to prove set laws by mutual inclusion, test relation properties from pairs/matrix/digraph, run Warshall's algorithm, classify equivalence classes and partitions, draw Hasse diagrams, and verify injective, surjective and bijective claims with proofs or counterexamples.

bank.q: Define a set and a subset. For sets A, B, C, prove A∩(B∪C)=(A∩B)∪(A∩C) by mutual inclusion, and verify the result with a membership table for A={1,2}, B={2,3}, C={3,4}.
outline: Correct definitions of set and subset.
Show every element of the left side lies in the right side.
Show every element of the right side lies in the left side.
Membership table columns for B∪C, A∩(B∪C), A∩B, A∩C and the union.
Conclude equality from matching columns.

bank.q: State the duality principle for set identities. Write the dual of (A∪B)ᶜ=Aᶜ∩Bᶜ and of A∪(B∩C)=(A∪B)∩(A∪C), then prove one dual identity element-wise.
outline: Duality swaps ∪ with ∩ and ∅ with U.
Correct dual expressions.
Element-wise proof using x∈ left iff x∈ right.
Mention universal set for complements.
Conclusion that the dual is also a valid identity.

bank.q: Define a relation on a set A and explain reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric and transitive properties using quantifiers. Give one example and one non-example for each property on A={1,2,3}.
outline: Definition R⊆A×A.
Quantifier form of each property.
Valid example for each property.
Non-example with the failing pair named.
Clear separation of antisymmetric from symmetric.

bank.q: Define equivalence relation, equivalence class and partition. State the theorem connecting equivalence relations on A with partitions of A, and illustrate it for congruence modulo 3 on the integers.
outline: Correct three definitions.
Statement of the bijection between equivalence relations and partitions.
Classes [0], [1], [2] modulo 3.
Disjointness and union equal to ℤ.
Conclusion that the classes form a partition.

bank.q: Let A={1,2,3,4} and R={(1,1),(1,2),(2,3),(3,1),(3,3),(4,4)}. Write the 0-1 matrix and digraph of R. Find which of reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric and transitive hold, giving a counterexample for each failure.
outline: Correct 4×4 0-1 matrix.
Correct directed edges in the digraph.
Check diagonal for reflexive.
Check reversed pairs for symmetric and antisymmetric.
Check triples for transitive and name missing pair.

bank.q: For R on A={1,2,3,4} given by pairs {(1,2),(2,3),(3,4)}, compute the reflexive closure, symmetric closure and transitive closure. Then run Warshall's algorithm on its 0-1 matrix and show each matrix after k=1,2,3,4.
outline: Reflexive closure adds (1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(4,4).
Symmetric closure adds reversed pairs.
Transitive closure adds (1,3),(1,4),(2,4).
Warshall matrices after each k.
Final reachability matrix matches transitive closure.

bank.q: Let A={1,2,3,6,12} ordered by divisibility. Draw the Hasse diagram. Find all maximal, minimal, greatest and least elements, and decide whether the poset is a total order.
outline: Covering pairs such as 1≺2, 1≺3, 2≺6, 3≺6, 6≺12.
Correct Hasse diagram with 12 at top and 1 at bottom.
Maximal element 12; minimal element 1.
Greatest 12 and least 1.
Not total because 2 and 3 are incomparable.

bank.q: Let f:ℤ→ℤ be f(n)=3n+1 and g:ℤ→ℤ be g(n)=n². Find f∘g and g∘f. Decide whether each of f, g, f∘g and g∘f is injective, surjective or bijective. Find inverses where they exist.
outline: Formulas (f∘g)(n)=3n²+1 and (g∘f)(n)=(3n+1)².
f is injective but not surjective; g is neither.
Compositions are neither injective nor surjective.
No inverse exists for any listed function on ℤ→ℤ.
Clear counterexamples for failures.

bank.q: Prove that a relation R on a nonempty set A is an equivalence relation if and only if its equivalence classes form a partition of A. Use the proof to explain why two different equivalence relations cannot give the same partition.
outline: Reflexivity makes each class nonempty and covers A.
Symmetry and transitivity make classes equal or disjoint.
Union of classes is A.
Converse: define x~y iff x and y lie in the same block.
Show the relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
Uniqueness of the relation from the partition.

bank.q: For a finite set A with n elements and a relation R on A, prove that the transitive closure is R∪R²∪…∪Rⁿ. Explain how Warshall's algorithm computes the same closure and why its running time is O(n³).
outline: Rᵏ means paths of length k.
A path of length more than n repeats a vertex.
Delete the repeated loop to shorten the path.
Hence lengths above n add no new pairs.
Warshall recurrence allows intermediate vertices 1 through k.
Triple loop gives n³ updates.

bank.q: A student claims every antisymmetric relation is asymmetric. Test the claim with a relation on A={1,2}, then state the correct implications among antisymmetric, asymmetric and irreflexive. Prove or disprove each implication.
outline: Equality relation is antisymmetric but not asymmetric.
Asymmetric implies antisymmetric.
Asymmetric implies irreflexive.
Irreflexive does not imply asymmetric.
Antisymmetric does not imply irreflexive.
Correct counterexamples for false implications.

bank.q: Let f:A→B and g:B→C. Prove that if g∘f is injective then f is injective, and if g∘f is surjective then g is surjective. Give counterexamples to show the converses fail.
outline: Definition of composition.
Injectivity proof: f(a₁)=f(a₂) gives g(f(a₁))=g(f(a₂)).
Surjectivity proof: every c is g(f(a)) for some a.
Counterexample where f is injective but g∘f is not.
Counterexample where g is surjective but g∘f is not.
Clear domains and codomains.

bank.q: Prove that a function f:A→B has an inverse f⁻¹:B→A if and only if f is bijective. For bijections f:A→B and g:B→C prove (g∘f)⁻¹=f⁻¹∘g⁻¹.
outline: Define inverse and both round-trip identities.
Injectivity is needed for uniqueness of preimage.
Surjectivity is needed so every b has a preimage.
Construct f⁻¹ when f is bijective.
Check domains and codomains in composition inverse.
Show (g∘f)⁻¹(c)=f⁻¹(g⁻¹(c)).

glossary.def: A collection of distinct objects where order and repetition are ignored.
A is a subset of B, written A⊆B, when every element of A belongs to B.
A∪B is the set of elements in A or B or both.
A∩B is the set of elements in both A and B.
Aᶜ is the set of elements in the universal set U that are not in A.
A△B is the set of elements in exactly one of A and B, so A△B=(A∖B)∪(B∖A).
A×B is the set of ordered pairs (a,b) with a∈A and b∈B.
A table with one row per element and one column per set, using 1 for membership and 0 otherwise.
A relation from A to B is a subset of A×B; a relation on A is a subset of A×A.
R on A is reflexive when (a,a)∈R for every a∈A.
R on A is symmetric when (a,b)∈R implies (b,a)∈R.
R on A is antisymmetric when (a,b)∈R and (b,a)∈R imply a=b.
R on A is transitive when (a,b)∈R and (b,c)∈R imply (a,c)∈R.
The transitive closure of R is the smallest transitive relation containing R; on a finite n-element set it is R∪R²∪…∪Rⁿ.
A triple-loop dynamic method that computes the transitive closure or reachability matrix of a relation in O(n³) time.
A relation on A that is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
For an equivalence relation ~, [a]={x∈A: x~a} is the class of a.
A collection of nonempty pairwise disjoint subsets of A whose union is A.
A reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive relation on A, usually written a≤b.
A drawing of a finite poset with an edge only for each covering pair a≺b, with b drawn above a.
A function f:A→B assigns exactly one element f(a)∈B to each a∈A.
A function f:A→B is injective when f(a)=f(b) implies a=b.
A function f:A→B is surjective when every b∈B equals f(a) for some a∈A.
A function that is both injective and surjective; it has an inverse.
For f:A→B and g:B→C, (g∘f):A→C is defined by (g∘f)(a)=g(f(a)).
For a bijection f:A→B, f⁻¹:B→A is defined by f⁻¹(b)=a exactly when f(a)=b.
